lesson.title: How steep is it

lead.text: To compare the two paths, share each climb out evenly over its ground. On the short path, 30 metres of climb happens over 15 metres of ground, so each metre along brings 30 ÷ 15 = 2 metres of climb. On the winding path the same 30 metres is spread over 60 metres of ground, which gives 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 metres of climb for each metre along.

Now the comparison is easy. 2 is four times as big as 0.5, so the short path is four times as steep. The number you get by dividing the climb by the distance along the ground is called the gradient. A gradient of 2 says the path climbs 2 metres for every 1 metre you cover.
Dividing is the whole method. It works for a hill, a ramp, a roof or a line on a grid, as long as you can find the climb and the distance along.
Share the climb out evenly over the ground, as you did for the two paths.

reveal.text: You divided the climb by the distance along the ground. That quotient is the gradient. Next the same idea goes onto the grid.

steps.headline: Rise and run on the grid

lead.text: Put a path on the grid and the two measurements need new names. Pick two points on the line and move from the first to the second. The change in y is called the rise, and the change in x is called the run. They are the climb and the distance along, in grid language, so the gradient is the rise divided by the run.
In the picture the line goes from A = (1, 2) to B = (4, 5). Across the grid it moves from x = 1 to x = 4, so the run is 4 − 1 = 3. Up the grid it moves from y = 2 to y = 5, so the rise is 5 − 2 = 3.

afterFigure.text: Both are 3, so the gradient is 3 ÷ 3 = 1. The line climbs one square for every square it moves across. You do not need the picture to get these numbers. Subtracting the coordinates of the two points gives the rise and the run, and the picture only shows what the subtraction means.

lead.text: Look at the two points. The rise is how far up you go from A to B.

reveal.text: That vertical change is the rise. Divide it by the run and you have the gradient.

lead.text: The picture helps when the points are close together, but the subtraction works anywhere. To get the rise, take the second point's y-coordinate and subtract the first point's. To get the run, do the same with the x-coordinates. From (2, 3) to (5, 9) the rise is 9 − 3 = 6 and the run is 5 − 2 = 3, so the gradient is 6 ÷ 3 = 2.

The order has to be the same in both subtractions. Reverse only one of them and the answer gets the wrong sign. A rise of 6 over a run of −3 would give −2, although the line really climbs. Each subtraction goes from the first point to the second, so both describe the same journey.
The next example takes a pair of points through the whole calculation, one line at a time.

workedSteps.text: Rise: subtract the y-coordinates, second minus first.
Run: subtract the x-coordinates in the same order.
Divide the rise by the run.
Rise: second y minus first y.
Run: second x minus first x.
Divide the rise by the run.

lead.text: So far every line has climbed as it moved to the right. A line can also fall. Take the points (0, 6) and (3, 0). Going from the first to the second, y drops from 6 to 0. The rise is 0 − 6 = −6 and the run is 3 − 0 = 3. That gives a gradient of −6 ÷ 3 = −2.

A negative rise means the line goes down, so the sign of the gradient tells you which way the line leans. A line that climbs as you move right has a positive gradient, and a line that falls has a negative gradient. A flat line has a rise of 0, and 0 divided by any run is 0, so its gradient is 0.

afterFigure.text: The size of the gradient, ignoring the sign, tells you how steep the line is. A gradient of 3 climbs faster than a gradient of 1/2, just as the short path climbed faster than the winding one. A gradient of −3 falls as quickly as 3 climbs.

lead.text: This line falls as it moves right. Keep the same order in both subtractions and watch the signs.

reveal.text: The rise came out negative and the run positive, so the gradient is negative, as the falling line showed.

lead.text: Not every line is steep. Keep the rise and the run apart until you divide.

lesson.orientation: Calculate a gradient from two points and say what its sign means.
lesson.nextAction: Draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and recover them from a drawn line.

blocks.text: Two points on a grid always have a straight line between them, and that line leans. Before measuring the lean on a grid, start somewhere you can feel it, which is a hillside. Say two paths lead from a car park to the same viewpoint, 30 metres higher up. One goes straight up the slope and covers 15 metres of ground on the way. The other winds gently and covers 60 metres.

Both paths climb the same height, yet the short one is far harder going. Neither number tells you how steep a path is on its own, because the steepness depends on the climb and the ground covered together.
This lesson turns that feeling into a single number. It starts with the paths and then moves the idea onto the grid from the last lesson. Lines that fall and lines that stay level come at the end.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a line's gradient from two points, and say what its sign tells you.

recap.keyIdea: The gradient is the rise divided by the run, taken in the same direction. Positive lines rise, negative lines fall and flat lines have gradient 0.

blocks.text: You compared two paths by sharing the climb over the ground, then found the gradient through (1, 2) and (3, 12) as 10 ÷ 2 = 5. The line through (−2, 3) and (2, −1) fell, so its gradient was −1.

recap.nextHook: A gradient says how steeply a line leans, but two lines with the same gradient can sit side by side at different heights. Next you'll see what fixes where a line sits, and how both numbers go into one equation.

questions.prompt: A path climbs 18 metres while you walk 6 metres along the ground. How many metres does it climb for each metre along the ground?
hints: Share the climb out evenly over the distance along the ground.
If you walk 6 metres and climb 18, what happens for just 1 metre?
Divide the climb by the distance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 metres of climb for each metre along.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Climb per step along is the idea behind gradient: how steep, in one number.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. For each metre means sharing the climb out.
That subtracts. Per metre means dividing the climb by the distance.

questions.prompt: How much does y increase from A = (0, 1) to B = (2, 5)?
hints: Read the vertical coordinates of A and B.
A has y = 1 and B has y = 5.
Subtract the starting height from the ending height.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The rise is the change in height: end y minus start y.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B's height. The increase is the change from A's height.
That adds the two heights. The increase is the difference between them.

Subtract the starting coordinate from the ending coordinate along each axis.
Divide the rise by the run in that order.
questions.onCorrect: 2. Rise ÷ run: the line goes up 2 for every 1 across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the run divided by the rise. The rise goes on top.
That is the rise on its own. Divide it by the run.

choices.label: Both changes must run from the first point to the second.

questions.prompt: Which line rises more for each step to the right?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A gradient of 3 means a rise of 3 for each unit moved to the right. Compare that rate with the smaller positive gradients.

questions.onCorrect: A gradient of 3 rises three for each step across: more than a smaller positive gradient.

misconceptions.feedback: A gradient of 1/2 rises only half a unit per step. Compare it with the other gradient.
A horizontal line does not rise at all.

hints: Both points have the same y-coordinate.
The vertical change is 4 − 4 while the horizontal change is nonzero.
Divide that vertical change by the horizontal run.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rise is 4 − 4 = 0; dividing by the run gives gradient 0.

questions.onCorrect: 0. The rise is zero, so the line is flat.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height. The rise is the change in height, and the height stays the same.
That compares the run with itself. Work out the rise first.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The run is the change in x, from the first point to the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rise, the change in y. The run is the change in x.

questions.prompt: A line goes through (1, 7) and (3, 1). Is its gradient positive, negative or zero?
questions.onCorrect: Negative: y goes down as x goes up, so the rise is negative and the run is positive.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the two heights. Does y go up or down as you move right?
The two heights differ, so the line is not flat.

citations.claim: The steepness of a path is its climb divided by the distance along the ground; that quotient is the slope (gradient).
Dividing the climb by the distance along gives the climb per unit along, which is the slope.
The slope of a line is the rise divided by the run, the change in y over the change in x between two points.
The rise between two points is the change in their y-coordinates.
Rise and run are found by subtracting coordinates in the same order: y2 − y1 over x2 − x1.
A line that rises to the right has positive slope, one that falls has negative slope, and a horizontal line has slope 0.
A climb of 18 over a run of 6 is 3 for each unit of run.
Rise and run are both taken from the first point to the second.
A larger positive slope rises more for each unit to the right.
